patterns.signal: A guard must notice the player only inside a view cone, and the code calls `acos` or `Vector3.Angle` per enemy per frame
patterns.use: Dot product against a precomputed cosine
patterns.why: With unit vectors, `dot(forward, toTarget) > cos(halfAngle)` is the cone test with no trig. Normalise both vectors first, or the comparison silently scales with distance.

patterns.signal: A homing missile or AI must decide whether to steer left or right toward a target
patterns.why: The sign of `cross(forward, toTarget)` along the up axis gives turn direction in one step. The sign convention flips with handedness, so verify it once in your engine.

patterns.signal: You need the facing normal of a triangle or a plane through three points
patterns.why: `normalize(cross(b - a, c - a))` is perpendicular to the surface. Its direction follows the winding order, so swapping two vertices flips the normal.

patterns.signal: A rotation tween drifts, spins the long way round, or behaves oddly once another axis nears 90 degrees
patterns.why: Quaternions avoid gimbal lock and interpolate along the shortest arc. Keep Euler angles for designer input and display only; renormalise quaternions after long chains of multiplications.

patterns.signal: Shading looks wrong on a mesh with non-uniform scale even though the silhouette is correct
patterns.why: Normals must be transformed by the inverse transpose of the model matrix to stay perpendicular to the surface. For uniform scale the plain rotation works and is cheaper.

patterns.signal: An object is skewed or orbits the origin instead of spinning in place after you build its matrix by hand
patterns.use: TRS order: scale, then rotate, then translate
patterns.why: With column vectors the world matrix is `T * R * S`, applied right to left. Matrix multiplication is not commutative, so any other order changes the result.

patterns.signal: A velocity or normal gets shifted when you push it through the same matrix as positions
patterns.use: w = 0 for directions, w = 1 for points
patterns.why: Homogeneous w makes translation apply to points only. Use the direction variant of the transform call; a direction transformed as a point picks up the object's position.

patterns.signal: A character or camera jitters only when it is tens of kilometres from the world origin
patterns.why: Float spacing grows with magnitude, so shift the world back toward zero when the player strays far. Costs a rebase step that must update physics, particles and networked positions consistently.

patterns.signal: A hot loop finds the nearest enemy by calling `Vector3.Distance` or `magnitude` on every candidate
patterns.why: Ordering is preserved without the square root: compare `sqrMagnitude` against `range * range`. Only take the root for the final value you actually display or use.

patterns.signal: A character should slide along a wall instead of stopping dead when moving into it
patterns.why: `v - dot(v, n) * n` removes the part of the motion into the surface and keeps the tangential part. `n` must be unit length, or the slide speed is wrong.

patterns.signal: Lighting changes when the object rotates, and the shader mixes an object-space normal with a world-space light direction
patterns.use: Do lighting in one consistent space
patterns.why: Transform every vector (normal, light, view) into the same space, usually world or view, before any dot product. Mixed spaces give plausible but wrong results that are hard to spot.

patterns.signal: Distant surfaces flicker in stripes (z-fighting) and the camera near plane is set to something like 0.01
patterns.why: Depth precision depends mostly on the near/far ratio, so raising near from 0.01 to 0.3 is the cheapest, biggest win. Too far out and nearby geometry clips through the camera.

patterns.signal: A huge view distance still z-fights after tuning near and far planes
patterns.use: Reversed-Z with a float depth buffer
patterns.why: Mapping far to 0 and near to 1 cancels float and 1/z nonlinearity, giving near-uniform precision. Every hand-written depth compare, clear value and depth read must use the reversed convention.

patterns.signal: A projected world-space label or marker shows up mirrored on screen when its target is behind the camera
patterns.use: Reject points with w <= 0 before dividing
patterns.why: A point behind the camera has negative clip w, and the divide mirrors it onto the screen. Check w first, then hide the marker or clamp it to the screen edge.

patterns.signal: A directional light shadow map, a 2D game or a top-down strategy view needs parallel lines and uniform scale
patterns.why: Ortho keeps w at 1, so size does not change with distance and depth is linear. It gives no depth cue, so it is wrong for first-person views.

patterns.signal: A fog or soft-particle effect reads the depth texture and treats the raw value as distance in metres
patterns.use: Linearise depth with near and far
patterns.why: Stored depth is a nonlinear function of 1/z and may be reversed. Convert it to linear eye depth first using the engine's helper, or effects bunch up near the camera.

patterns.signal: A screen-space effect needs the world position of each pixel but there is no position buffer
patterns.why: Combine pixel UV and depth into NDC, then multiply by the inverse view-projection and divide by w. Saves a G-buffer target at the cost of a matrix multiply per pixel.

patterns.signal: A click or tap on the screen must select the 3D object under the cursor
patterns.use: Unproject a ray from the camera
patterns.why: Map the pixel to NDC at near and far depth, transform both by the inverse view-projection, and raycast between them. Avoids per-object screen-space tests.

patterns.signal: A prop's imported vertex count is three or four times what the DCC tool reports
patterns.use: Split vertices only at hard edges and UV seams
patterns.why: Every unique attribute combination is its own GPU vertex. Soften edges that do not need to be hard and merge UV islands where stretching is acceptable; keep real seams.

patterns.signal: A mesh is stored as a triangle soup where shared corners are duplicated in the vertex buffer
patterns.why: An index buffer shares vertices between triangles, cutting memory and vertex shader runs. Only vertices with fully identical attributes can be shared.

patterns.signal: A GPU capture shows the vertex stage is heavy and the mesh's ACMR is well above 1
patterns.why: Reordering triangles (for example with meshoptimizer) raises post-transform cache hits, so fewer vertex shader runs per triangle. The image is unchanged; it does nothing for fragment cost.

patterns.signal: Vertex buffers dominate mesh memory and every attribute is stored as 32-bit float
patterns.why: Normals and tangents as snorm8 and UVs as unorm16 can halve the stride. Keep positions at full float when far from the origin, since half floats get coarse quickly.

patterns.signal: A procedural mesh with more than 65,535 vertices renders as scrambled spikes
patterns.use: 32-bit index format or split the mesh
patterns.why: 16-bit indices wrap past 65,535. Set the index format (`Mesh.indexFormat` in Unity) before assigning triangles, or chunk the mesh; 32-bit indices double index memory.

patterns.signal: A normal-mapped mesh shows seams along UV borders and inverted bumps on its mirrored half
patterns.use: Match the tangent basis to the baker
patterns.why: Import tangents in the same convention the map was baked with, usually MikkTSpace, including the w sign for mirroring. Recalculating with a different method breaks the bake.

patterns.signal: Distant characters with dense meshes make the frame fragment-bound because triangles are smaller than a pixel
patterns.why: Swap to simpler meshes as screen size shrinks, cutting wasted 2x2 quad shading and vertex work. Costs memory and authoring time, and needs crossfade or hysteresis to hide popping.

patterns.signal: A skinned or vertex-displaced mesh vanishes near the screen edge even though part of it is visible
patterns.why: Culling uses the bounding box, which does not know about shader displacement or animation reach. Enlarge it to cover the full motion; too large wastes culling efficiency.

patterns.signal: Waves, flags or grass sway are animated by rewriting vertex positions on the CPU every frame
patterns.why: A time-driven vertex shader avoids per-frame CPU work and buffer uploads. Bounds must be expanded, and CPU-side physics will not see the deformed shape.

patterns.signal: A teammate proposes a shader optimisation, but nobody has compared CPU and GPU frame times yet
patterns.use: Measure both sides, fix the long pole
patterns.why: CPU and GPU run as a pipeline, so the frame takes as long as the slower one. Saving GPU time in a CPU-bound frame changes nothing but power use.

patterns.signal: Code reads a render texture or buffer back to the CPU mid-frame and the frame is longer than CPU plus GPU work alone
patterns.why: A synchronous read makes the CPU wait for the GPU to drain. An async request returns a frame or more later, so the logic must tolerate stale data.

patterns.signal: A capture shows heavy opaque overdraw: the same pixels shaded several times per frame
patterns.use: Sort opaque draws front to back
patterns.why: Near objects fill the depth buffer first, so early-Z rejects hidden fragments before shading. Conflicts with sorting by state, so engines sort by a key that balances both.

patterns.signal: Opaque fragment shaders are expensive and overdraw stays high even after sorting, for example dense foliage
patterns.why: Render depth only first, then shade with an equal depth test so each pixel is shaded once. Doubles vertex work and draw calls, so it pays only when fragment cost dominates.

patterns.signal: An opaque shader uses `discard`/`clip` or writes depth, and overdraw cost jumped
patterns.why: Discard and depth writes force late depth testing, so hidden fragments get shaded. Restrict them to cutout materials, render those after plain opaques, or use a depth prepass.

patterns.signal: Objects far outside the camera view still appear as draw calls in the frame debugger
patterns.why: Test bounding volumes against the view frustum before submission to skip CPU and GPU work. Needs correct bounds; large meshes that span the view are never culled, so split them.

patterns.signal: Indoor or city levels draw many objects that are fully hidden behind walls or buildings
patterns.why: Baked visibility data or a depth-pyramid test skips hidden draws. It costs CPU or GPU time and memory itself, so it pays only in scenes with heavy occlusion.

patterns.signal: A fragment shader that uses many registers runs slower than a longer but leaner shader
patterns.why: Fewer registers per thread lets more warps stay resident to hide texture latency. Shorten live ranges or split passes; verify the occupancy gain in a GPU profiler.

patterns.signal: The fragment shader computes a value that varies linearly across the triangle, such as a fog factor or a scaled UV
patterns.use: Move work from fragment to vertex shader
patterns.why: Vertices are far fewer than pixels, and interpolation delivers the result for free. Only for values that are linear across a triangle; per-pixel lighting detail gets lost.

patterns.signal: An `if` on per-pixel data like noise or a texture value saves nothing in profiles
patterns.use: Branch on uniforms, not per-pixel data
patterns.why: A divergent warp runs both paths. Branch on material or per-draw constants, or use branchless `lerp`/`step` for small bodies; coherent per-pixel branches over large areas can still pay off.

patterns.signal: A texture fetch sits inside a per-pixel branch and edge pixels show blocky mip artefacts
patterns.why: Implicit derivatives are undefined when neighbouring pixels in a quad take different paths. Sample before the branch, or pass explicit gradients or a mip level.

patterns.signal: A shader declares many independent `multi_compile` keywords and builds are slow and memory heavy
patterns.use: Variant budget: fewer keywords plus stripping
patterns.why: Variants multiply per keyword. Use `shader_feature` for material-only toggles, strip unused combinations in builds, and move cheap toggles to uniform branches.

patterns.signal: The game freezes once, for a few hundred ms, the first time a new effect or material appears
patterns.why: The driver compiles the variant or pipeline state on first use. Collect the variants actually used and precompile them during loading; costs load time and needs maintaining.

patterns.signal: A fragment shader evaluates an expensive function of one or two inputs every pixel, like a BRDF term or colour curve
patterns.why: Bake the function into a small 1D/2D/3D texture and sample it. Trades ALU for a fetch and memory, and loses precision between texels, so it suits smooth functions.

patterns.signal: The CPU uploads tightly packed floats but the shader reads the second `float3` from the wrong offset
patterns.why: Constant buffers align fields to 16-byte rows. Lay out data as `float4` groups or add explicit padding so CPU and GPU structs match exactly.

patterns.signal: Per-object, per-material and per-frame constants are all uploaded together in one buffer every draw
patterns.why: Separate per-frame, per-material and per-draw buffers so each is uploaded only when it changes, reducing bandwidth and binding cost on the CPU.

patterns.signal: Lighting looks darker in the middle of large triangles even though vertex normals are unit length
patterns.why: Linear interpolation of unit vectors shortens them between vertices. Call `normalize` in the fragment shader; one cheap instruction per pixel.

patterns.signal: An integer material ID or index passed to the fragment stage gets blended into garbage between vertices
patterns.why: Mark the attribute `nointerpolation` so every fragment gets the provoking vertex's value. Requires all vertices of the triangle to carry the same ID.

patterns.signal: Thousands of independent elements (particles, culling, simulation) are updated in a C# loop each frame
patterns.use: Move data-parallel work to a compute shader
patterns.why: The GPU processes elements in parallel and the data stays on the GPU for rendering. Reading results back costs latency; the gain needs many elements and little branching.

patterns.signal: Distant ground textures shimmer and crawl as the camera moves slowly
patterns.why: Minified textures skip texels and alias; mips prefilter them and improve cache hits. Costs about 33 percent more memory; skip only for textures never minified, like pixel-exact UI.

patterns.signal: A road or floor turns into a blurry smear at grazing angles while surfaces facing the camera look sharp
patterns.why: Takes extra samples along the stretched axis instead of dropping to a blurry mip. Costs bandwidth, so use 4x to 16x on ground textures and leave it off elsewhere.

patterns.signal: Texture memory is over budget and most textures are stored as uncompressed RGBA8
patterns.why: BC on desktop and console, ASTC on modern mobile, ETC2 as a fallback; textures stay compressed in VRAM at 4x to 8x savings. Lossy, so check normal maps and gradients.

patterns.signal: Roughness, metallic and AO are each a separate greyscale texture per material
patterns.why: Store each mask in one channel of a single texture, cutting fetches and memory. All channels share one resolution and compression, and the packed texture must be linear.

patterns.signal: Normal maps or roughness masks look subtly wrong, with flat or overly bright lighting on slopes
patterns.use: sRGB for colour, linear for data
patterns.why: The sRGB flag decodes gamma on sample, which is right for albedo and wrong for normals, masks and LUTs. Set it per texture by what the data means, not by how it looks.

patterns.signal: Hundreds of small UI icons or sprites each use their own texture and break batching
patterns.why: One texture lets many elements share a material and batch. Pad and extrude edges against bleeding at lower mips; atlases cannot use wrap-mode tiling per element.

patterns.signal: Terrain layers or tiling materials need per-layer wrap and mips but you want one material and one binding
patterns.why: Each slice keeps its own wrap, mips and filtering with no bleeding, indexed by a slice number. All slices must share size and format.

patterns.signal: Normal maps show blocky banding after compression with a generic colour format
patterns.why: Store X and Y in a two-channel format (BC5 or ASTC with normal settings) and rebuild Z in the shader. Higher quality per bit, at the cost of a few ALU instructions.

patterns.signal: A large open world cannot keep every texture's full mip chain resident in memory
patterns.why: Load only the mip levels each texture needs at its current screen size, keeping a memory budget. Textures may look blurry briefly while higher mips stream in.

patterns.signal: Static level geometry needs soft indirect light and the real-time lighting cost is too high
patterns.why: Precompute direct and indirect light into textures, so runtime cost is one fetch. Lights and geometry must stay static; bakes cost iteration time and lightmap memory.

patterns.signal: A moving character stays brightly lit when walking from a sunny courtyard into a baked dark corridor
patterns.why: Probes sample baked indirect light at points in space, and dynamic objects interpolate between them. Place them densely where light changes, especially at doorways and shadow edges.

patterns.signal: Shiny objects reflect the sky indoors, or reflections do not line up with the room's walls
patterns.why: Place probes per area so reflections show the local surroundings; box projection aligns them with room walls. Real-time probe updates are expensive, so bake them where possible.

patterns.signal: Sun shadows are blocky near the camera because one shadow map covers the whole view distance
patterns.why: Split the view frustum into ranges, each with its own shadow map, so near shadows get the resolution. Each cascade adds a shadow render pass; also cap shadow distance.

patterns.signal: Shadows show stripy self-shadowing (acne), or they float detached from the feet (peter-panning)
patterns.why: Acne means too little bias; detached shadows mean too much. Use a small depth bias plus normal-offset bias, and tune per light rather than raising one value.

patterns.signal: Artists retune shininess per scene because materials look right under one lighting setup and wrong under another
patterns.why: An energy-conserving BRDF with measurable parameters keeps materials consistent under any light. Needs reference values and linear-space lighting to pay off.

patterns.signal: A metal surface looks like dull grey plastic even with low roughness
patterns.why: Metals need metallic = 1 with the tint in base colour; dielectrics need metallic = 0. In-between values are only for transitions such as rust or dirt edges.

patterns.signal: Surface detail like bricks or scratches is needed but the triangle budget is already spent
patterns.why: Fakes shading detail at a texture fetch per pixel. Silhouettes and grazing views stay flat, so large forms still need real geometry or parallax techniques.

patterns.signal: Many point and spot lights cast real-time shadows and shadow rendering dominates the GPU frame
patterns.why: Point lights render up to six shadow faces each. Limit shadowed lights to the few that matter, bake the rest, and cull shadow casters by distance.

patterns.signal: Dozens of small overlapping point lights tank a classic forward renderer, which is GPU-bound
patterns.use: Deferred or forward+ for many lights
patterns.why: Deferred lights a G-buffer once per light volume; forward+ builds per-tile light lists. Deferred costs bandwidth and complicates MSAA and transparency, so forward+ often suits mid-range.

patterns.signal: A mobile or VR game uses few lights, needs MSAA, and is bandwidth constrained
patterns.why: No G-buffer, so far less bandwidth, and MSAA works directly. Cost scales with objects times lights, so keep per-object light counts low.

patterns.signal: Transparent objects render in the wrong order and pop in front of each other as the camera moves
patterns.why: Alpha blending is order-dependent, so draw far to near after opaques. Per-object sorting fails for intersecting or self-overlapping meshes; split those meshes.

patterns.signal: Interpenetrating transparent surfaces flicker even with per-object sorting
patterns.why: Weighted blended OIT or per-pixel lists remove the sort dependency. Approximate or memory heavy, so use only where sorting cannot be fixed by splitting geometry.

patterns.signal: Foliage or fences use alpha blending, sort badly and cause heavy overdraw
patterns.why: Treat them as opaque with `clip` so they write depth and need no sorting. Loses soft edges and early-Z; alpha-to-coverage smooths edges when MSAA is on.

patterns.signal: Particle effects with large mostly transparent quads make the GPU fill-rate bound when the camera gets close
patterns.why: Use tighter mesh-shaped sprites, cap particle count and size near the camera, or render particles to a lower-resolution buffer. Low-res buffers need careful upsampling at edges.

patterns.signal: Bloom looks weak and a bright sun glows the same as a white shirt
patterns.why: Without HDR all bright values clip at 1.0, so bloom cannot tell them apart. HDR targets cost bandwidth; tonemap once at the end of the chain.

patterns.signal: Thin wires and shiny specular highlights shimmer in a deferred renderer when the camera moves
patterns.why: TAA accumulates jittered samples over frames, fixing both geometry and shader aliasing. Needs correct motion vectors and can ghost or blur; MSAA only fixes geometry edges.

patterns.signal: A GPU-bound frame at high resolution must get faster and dropping native resolution looks too soft
patterns.why: Render fewer pixels and reconstruct with history and motion vectors. Saves GPU fragment time only; it does nothing for a CPU-bound frame and can ghost on bad motion vectors.

patterns.signal: Vignette, colour grading, grain and tonemapping each run as a separate full-screen pass
patterns.use: Merge post effects into an uber pass
patterns.why: One pass reads and writes the frame once instead of several times, saving bandwidth, especially on mobile. Effects that need neighbouring pixels, like blur, still need their own passes.

patterns.signal: The frame is GPU-bound and you need to know whether pixel work is the cause
patterns.why: Halve the render resolution: a big drop means fragment or fill-rate bound. Almost no change points at vertex work, CPU submission or fixed-cost passes.

patterns.signal: Halving resolution barely helps a GPU-bound frame that is full of dense meshes
patterns.use: Cut vertex work: LODs, culling, simpler skinning
patterns.why: Vertex cost does not scale with resolution. Confirm in a capture that the vertex stage is busy before reducing triangle counts or skinned bone influences.

patterns.signal: Thousands of copies of the same mesh and material are drawn as separate draw calls and the render thread is busy
patterns.why: One draw submits many copies with per-instance data in a buffer, cutting CPU submission cost. Needs the same mesh and material; per-instance variation must go through instance data.

patterns.signal: Many different static meshes share a few materials and the CPU spends its time on draw submission
patterns.use: Batch and sort draws by state
patterns.why: Combine static meshes or sort draws by shader, then material, so state changes are rare. Static batching costs memory and coarsens culling; state changes cost more than triangles.

patterns.signal: The render thread is pegged on one core while other cores sit idle, on an explicit API
patterns.why: D3D12, Vulkan and Metal let several threads record command buffers in parallel. Requires explicit sync and resource-state tracking; the engine usually exposes it as a setting.

patterns.signal: A mobile game starts at 60 fps, drops to 40 after a minute and the device heats up
patterns.use: Profile sustained performance and cap frame rate
patterns.why: Thermal throttling cuts clocks after the device heats. Test over many minutes, budget below peak, and use a lower frame-rate cap or fewer passes to save power.

patterns.signal: A mobile GPU timeline shows many full-screen passes that read and write the same render targets
patterns.use: Keep render passes merged on tile GPUs
patterns.why: Each pass switch flushes tile memory to DRAM and reloads it. Merge passes, use subpasses or framebuffer fetch, and avoid mid-frame target switches; bandwidth is the scarce resource.

patterns.signal: Each render pass on mobile loads the previous target contents and stores depth that is never read again
patterns.why: Loading and storing whole attachments costs bandwidth on tile GPUs. Clear or discard on load, discard depth and MSAA samples on store, using memoryless attachments where possible.

patterns.signal: A character renders black on one device only, and frame timings do not explain it
patterns.use: Frame capture in RenderDoc or Xcode
patterns.why: A capture shows each draw's bound shaders, textures, constants and render state, so you can see the wrong input. It costs capture overhead and shows one frame, not trends.
